narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 54.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile of your class that year, far below the average ranking of students who were accepted. This low standing signaled to the model a higher risk that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked in the opposite direction, pulling the prediction toward passing. At 36, your score sits only slightly below the average of 37.2 among accepted students, so the model saw this as a modest positive.

Your undergraduate GPA came in third. At 3.0 it is also modestly below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants and therefore nudged the outcome slightly toward failure.

Taken together, the model concluded that your relatively weak class ranking in year three outweighed the small positives from your LSAT and GPA, tipping the scales past the 50% failure threshold.

What you should do next is straightforward: strengthen the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retake the LSAT if possible, or consider a post-baccalaureate program that can demonstrably improve both your GPA and class ranking before reapplying. These steps would directly address the factors that led to the rejection. (248 words)
